# StackVitals

> A free, GitHub-native engineering health suite: one GitHub Action keeps CI, pull request, delivery (DORA), community and dependency history on a data branch in your own repo, with a static app, a CLI and an MCP server over it. No server of ours, no Docker.

## Facts

- Runs as a GitHub Action in your own repo: no server of ours, no Docker, no account; history is kept on a `stackvitals-data` branch in the same repo.
- Reads GitHub's API with the workflow's own token: Actions runs, jobs, logs and test reports, pull requests, reviews, releases and deployments. It doesn't use git hooks and doesn't point at lines of code.
- On a pull request whose CI failed, one comment sorts each failure: likely flaky, already failing on main, new, and a few more; no verdict passes the check by itself.
- Deployments come from GitHub's Deployments API, deploy workflows and releases, found without setup, and from any other tool (Argo CD, Jenkins, a shell script) through `stackvitals record` or a `repository_dispatch` event.
- It acts as well as reports: alerts to Slack, Teams, Discord or a webhook, opt-in re-runs of flaky jobs, issues, quarantine, suggested reviewers and size labels.
- Optional connectors: Jira, Linear, PagerDuty, incident.io, Slack and Discord channels, Discourse, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps, SonarQube, test reports from Jenkins, CircleCI and Buildkite, AI spend.
- SQL over the history in the browser and with `stackvitals sql`; an export with DevLake's table names for Postgres; Backstage catalog entities with the repo's level as an annotation (no card inside Backstage).
- Speaks CDEvents: deployments, rollbacks and incidents come in as CDEvents or from Flux; alerts, newly flaky tests and pull request verdicts go out as CDEvents custom events, to a URL or as repository_dispatch.
- An MCP server gives AI agents the same history and verdicts.
- Every verdict's rule is checked on public data and the misses are published.

## Docs

- [How accurate StackVitals is](docs/accuracy.md): The rules behind StackVitals' verdicts and headline numbers were each checked against public data and, where a judgement was needed, against labelled examples.
- [The StackVitals app](docs/app.md): Every run publishes one app over all the modules that ran: https://OWNER.github.io/REPO/ once GitHub Pages serves the stackvitals-data branch.
- [How StackVitals works](docs/architecture.md): StackVitals has no hosted backend.
- [What StackVitals reads, and from where](docs/connectors.md): Live means run against the real service; recorded means tested against saved answers in the shape the service's documentation gives, with no account of ours; experimental means built but not yet checked either way.
- [Coverage and peer groups](docs/coverage.md): When StackVitals compares your repo with "similar public repos", the peers come from the project's crawler (built for MergeScout, the Contribute module, and now feeding every benchmark), which reads public GitHub...
- [Using delivery numbers without fooling yourself](docs/dora-guide.md): DORA's numbers describe a team's delivery system, not a person's work.
- [Questions people ask](docs/faq.md): It is licensed under Apache 2.0 and runs in your own GitHub Actions minutes, which are free for public repos and included in every plan for private ones.
- [StackVitals for an open-source maintainer](docs/guides/maintainer.md): You want red CI to stop eating contributors' time, newcomers answered, and fewer surprise dependency breaks.
- [StackVitals for an engineering manager](docs/guides/manager.md): You want to know where your team's time goes and whether changes help, without rating people.
- [StackVitals for a platform team](docs/guides/platform.md): You run GitHub for an org and want one view of every repo, owners that are real, standards people can see coming, and a security review you can sign off.
- [Install](docs/install.md): StackVitals has two parts: a GitHub Action, uses: stackvitals/stackvitals@v0, that runs in your repo, and the stackvitals command on your machine, which sets the Action up, opens a private repo's dashboard and runs...
- [Known limitations](docs/limitations.md): What each part of StackVitals can't see or do, where its measured accuracy is weak, and what it needs from your repo.
- [Methods: the exact settings behind every number](docs/methods.md): Every headline number in StackVitals carries its sample size and a 95% range.
- [Modules](docs/modules.md): What each StackVitals module does, how to try it on any public repo from your machine, and how to set it up in your own repo.
- [What leaves your repo](docs/privacy.md): StackVitals runs in your own workflow and keeps its history in your repo.
- [Quick start: your monitor in about five minutes](docs/quickstart.md): A GitHub repo is all you need; CI on GitHub Actions makes the CI part useful.
- [Rule reference](docs/rules.md): Every rule a StackVitals verdict or number rests on, from bench/accuracy/registry.json: what it does, the data it was tuned on and checked on, the bar it had to meet (set before the check where a date says so), its...
- [How StackVitals grows with you](docs/scaling.md): StackVitals keeps each repo's history in that repo's own stackvitals-data branch.
- [StackVitals settings](docs/settings.md): Put these in .github/stackvitals.toml on your default branch.
- [Model triage: setup](docs/triage.md): When StackVitals' history and the log's signs can't decide whether a pull request's failure came from the change, a model can read the failing step's error lines and the changed file names and give its view.

## Compared with

- [StackVitals and CDviz](docs/compare/cdviz.md): CDviz: Delivery observability built on CDEvents, the CD Foundation's event standard: a collector, Postgres with TimescaleDB, and Grafana.
- [StackVitals and Apache DevLake](docs/compare/devlake.md): Apache DevLake: A data platform that collects DevOps data from about 50 tools into one model and shows it in Grafana, with DORA's five metrics.
- [StackVitals and Faros Community Edition](docs/compare/faros-community-edition.md): Faros Community Edition: An engineering-operations platform (Airbyte, Postgres, Hasura, Metabase, dbt, n8n).
- [StackVitals and Trunk Flaky Tests and BuildPulse](docs/compare/flaky-test-tools.md): Trunk Flaky Tests and BuildPulse: Flaky-test services: they read JUnit reports from CI, detect flaky tests and quarantine them.
- [StackVitals and GrimoireLab](docs/compare/grimoirelab.md): GrimoireLab: CHAOSS's software-analytics toolset: 30+ sources, identity merging and community-health dashboards.
- [StackVitals and Liatrio's DORA plugin for Backstage](docs/compare/liatrio-backstage.md): Liatrio's DORA plugin for Backstage: A Backstage plugin showing DORA metrics per service.
- [StackVitals and LinearB](docs/compare/linearb.md): LinearB: A commercial engineering-metrics product with DORA, and gitStream rules that automate pull requests.
- [StackVitals and Middleware](docs/compare/middleware.md): Middleware: An open-source DORA app (middlewarehq/middleware) with its own web UI.
- [StackVitals and Pelorus](docs/compare/pelorus.md): Pelorus: A Red Hat community project measuring DORA's four metrics with Prometheus exporters and Grafana.
- [StackVitals compared with other tools](docs/compare/README.md): What each tool does better, what StackVitals does differently, and what was measured side by side.
- [StackVitals and Swarmia](docs/compare/swarmia.md): Swarmia: A commercial engineering-effectiveness product: DORA, developer surveys, AI-adoption tracking and software capitalization.

## Optional

- [StackVitals and CHAOSS](docs/chaoss.md): CHAOSS defines open source community health metrics.
- [Enterprise controls](docs/enterprise.md): StackVitals has no server and no account: it runs in your GitHub Actions with your tokens and keeps everything in your repos.
- [Release checklist](docs/release-checklist.md): Run this before tagging a release.
- [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md): What comes next, in rough order.
- [Threat model](docs/threat-model.md): StackVitals runs inside your own GitHub Actions with your repo's tokens, reads text that strangers write (pull request titles, test names, logs, issues, comments) and writes back to GitHub (comments, labels, issues,...
